the same direction as the sort field (this is the ordering your README already documents: "ties are broken by `id` in the same direction"). The ordering is now a total order with exactly one position per row, so "strictly after the cursor" is always well-defined. It also makes `desc` the exact reverse of `asc`, which the old `_seq` tie-break broke for ties.
- **`src/cursor.js`** — returns `{ sortKey, id }`, and validates the payload is a 2-element array. Cursor format is unchanged and still opaque base64url `[sortKey, id]`.

`listPage`'s resume logic needed no change: its probe now compares correctly because the comparator honours `id`.

## Verification beyond the suite

I wrote a throwaway property check (since deleted — nothing added to your repo) with an **independent oracle** written from the README contract rather than from `src/sort.js`, then checked 200 random datasets (heavy score ties, 1–25 rows, ids deliberately non-lexicographic so `id10` vs `id2` is exercised) against every page size 1…n+2 in both directions: every row exactly once, in contract order, each page equal to its slice of the global order, `_seq` stripped, limit respected, source array not mutated. Plus: all-rows-tied, a cursor whose row was deleted mid-tie (resumes without skip or repeat), end-of-list empty page with `nextCursor: null`, and input-not-mutated.

Three of my own assertions were wrong along the way and each was worth the catch — `id10` sorting before `id2` is the documented contract, not a bug.

**One boundary I deliberately left alone:** a falsy cursor (`null`, `undefined`, `''`) is treated as "from the top", which is pre-existing behaviour and what callers passing an empty query param rely on. I did not tighten it to throw. **Unchecked:** nothing in CI beyond `npm test`; if you have a downstream consumer that persisted cursors before this change, old cursors still decode (the `id` was always in the payload — it was only being dropped on read), so no cursor migration is needed.
